lesson.title: Edge Computing: When the Cloud Is Too Far Away
lesson.summary: Edge computing pushes computation, not just cached content, out of the centralized network core and onto servers physically close to where data is generated, cutting the round trip time a distant cloud data center would require.
lesson.body:
A CDN moves cached content closer to users, but it only caches things, static files that do not change based on who is asking or what is happening right now. Edge computing takes the same underlying instinct, get physically closer to the user or the data source, and applies it to something CDNs do not do: running actual computation, not just serving cached files, on servers positioned near the edge of the network rather than back in a distant, centralized data center reached through the network core.

Centralized cloud computing puts heavy computation in a small number of very large, efficient data centers, which works extremely well for a huge range of workloads. But reaching one of those centralized data centers, through the network core and across whatever distance separates the user from it, takes real time, routinely tens of milliseconds, sometimes more depending on distance and network conditions. For many applications that is completely fine. For a growing set of applications, it is not. Edge computing responds by placing smaller compute facilities much closer to where data is generated or where a decision needs to be made, sometimes as close as a nearby cell tower or a facility on site, trading the efficiency of full centralization for a dramatically shorter round trip.

Self driving vehicles are the example that makes the stakes obvious. When a car's perception system detects a pedestrian stepping into the road, the decision to brake cannot wait for a request to travel to a data center that might be hundreds of miles away and back, that round trip alone, even before any processing happens, could take longer than the vehicle has to react safely. That kind of decision has to be made either onboard the vehicle itself or at an edge server close enough that the round trip fits within a latency budget of just a few milliseconds. Industrial settings raise similar demands: sensors on factory equipment feeding a real time control loop that needs to react to a fault within milliseconds cannot tolerate a round trip to a distant cloud region either.

Edge computing and CDNs frequently share physical infrastructure, points of presence positioned near users are a natural place to add general purpose compute capacity alongside content caching, and many CDN providers have expanded into offering edge compute for exactly this reason. The distinction that matters conceptually is what is happening at that nearby location: a CDN node serves files it already has, while an edge computing node can run arbitrary logic, make decisions, and process data that is specific to the moment, closer to where that data was generated than a centralized cloud region could ever be.
